newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says security better if settlers leave Hebron.
newsitem.headline: PLO says security better if settlers leave Hebron.

text.p: Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation failed in talks on Wednesday to reach any agreement on thorny issues, but Israel's chief negotiator said at least mutual accusations were set aside.
Palestinian negotiators went into a meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat after the talks and were not immediately available for comment.
Talks resume on Thursday in the Israeli-controlled area of Gaza near the border with the Jewish state.
Earlier on Wednesday, the chief Palestinian negotiator said Israel could break a deadlock over the West Bank town of Hebron by removing 400 militant Jewish settlers from its centre.

"A serious and detailed discussion has taken place," an Israeli participant at the meetings at Beit Hanoun in the Palestinian self-rule enclave in the Gaza Strip quoted Israeli delegation head Dan Shomron as saying.
Shomron said though no agreement had been reached but "mutual accusations had been laid aside".

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, mediating at the talks, played down the conflicting positions over Israel's long-delayed thinning of forces in Hebron. "They are making a serious effort to understand each other's concerns," he said.

Israel agreed more than a year ago to redeploy in Hebron by March of this year but delayed after Palestinian bombers killed 59 people in Israel. Hebron has 100,000 Arabs, plus 400 Jewish settlers determined to stay in the heart of the town and 5,500 in the nearby settlement of Kiryat Arba.
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said earlier on Wednesday the Hebron talks, which opened on Sunday, were deadlocked. Fifty-nine Arabs and 15 Israelis died in an outbreak of violence last month.

"One of the easy solutions to the security concerns of Israelis who are trying to change the Hebron agreement under the pretext of offering additional security...is to move settlers from the city centre to the nearby Kiryat Arba settlement," Erekat told Reuters.
Erekat said Israeli negotiators were trying to rewrite the agreement the previous Israeli government signed.

Although tension has eased since the bloodshed triggered by Israel opening a controversial tunnel near Islamic holy sites in Jerusalem, Palestinian officials in self-ruled Gaza said none of the 10,000 workers Israel said could go to jobs on Wednesday had been allowed into the Jewish state.

"The Israelis have informed us that they will allow 10,000 workers from Gaza to go to work. But it takes time to issue entry permits," said Said al-Mudallal, director of employment at the Palestinian Ministry of Labour. He said he did not expect any workers to enter before Friday.

Palestinian officials earlier had said the Israeli delegation to the Hebron talks proposed changes that would reduce the number of Palestinian police allowed in Hebron and insisted they be armed with pistols rather than rifles.
The Israelis also wanted to keep control of parts of the town due to be transferred to the Palestinians under the existing agreement, which the Jewish settlers oppose.
Erekat countered that Palestinians had their own security concerns because of the militant settlers. A Jewish settler massacred 29 Palestinian worshippers at Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque in 1994.

"Of course nobody said it was going to be easy," the Israeli source said. "What we're proposing is to operate within the boundaries of the agreement but to take into account our security considerations."
Ross said in Gaza after seeing Arafat: "We are going to do all we can to help them make progress...I think we have to be patient,but determined and try to produce as quickly as we can."
